issues: '46.1% of the most popular websites in every EU member state' can be read as 46.1% in each state. It is the pooled figure for the 500 most popular sites of each of the 28 member states. Degeling's Table III shows January 2018 rates by country list ranging from about 9.5% (Estonia) to 53.9% (Poland).

'and most did not meet the law's own standard for consent' overgeneralises. The only support is Nouwens et al.: a September 2019 scrape of 680 top-10,000 UK sites that used the five most popular consent platforms, of which 11.8% met three minimal requirements. That is a different population and year from the EU-wide 2018 banners in the sentence. The fix states the finding with its scope.

Source 1's quote stops at 'to state that' and so never shows the consent requirement it is cited for. It is extended to the verbatim continuation (--check FOUND). The primary text of Directive 2009/136/EC Art. 2(5) (amended Art. 5(3)) is added from legislation.gov.uk.
'62.1% by the end of May 2018' is right. Degeling's section VI says '62.1 % at the end of May (post-GDPR)'. That quote is added.
Degeling's own domain count is internally inconsistent (6,579 in the abstract, 6,759 in the body), so no domain total is used in the fix.

fieldFixes.correction: Cookie consent predates the GDPR: a 2009 amendment (Directive 2009/136/EC) to the EU's ePrivacy Directive already made storing information on a user's device conditional on consent (strictly necessary cookies excepted), and in January 2018, months before the GDPR applied on 25 May 2018, 46.1% of the sites on the 500-most-popular lists of the 28 EU member states already showed a cookie consent notice. The GDPR accelerated them, to 62.1% by the end of May 2018. Many still fell short of the law's own standard for consent: a September 2019 scrape of 680 top UK sites using the five most popular consent platforms found only 11.8% met minimal requirements of EU law.

sourceFixes.note: Fresh fetch 2026-09-23, --check FOUND. Method: '500 most popular websites in each of the 28 member states of the EU', inspected manually in January and May 2018.

issues: The numbers are right: 11.8% met the three conditions (explicit consent, reject as easy as accept, no pre-ticked optional boxes); 50.1% had no 'reject all' button; removing the reject-all button from the first page raised consent by 22-23 percentage points (0.220 and 0.231 slopes).

'scraped the five most popular consent platforms on the top 10,000 UK sites in 2019' leaves out that the percentages cover the 680 sites where those CMPs were found, not 10,000 sites. The scrape date (September 2019) is added.
'in their experiment' leaves out that it was a 40-participant field experiment. That matters for how much weight the 22-23 point effect can bear.

'Design, not preference, drives much of the "yes"' overstates the finding. The paper's regressions attribute 11.7% (barrier) and 13.5% (banner) of the variation in answers to button prominence. It is softened to what the paper shows.
Source 1 claims 'Only 12.6% ... same or fewer number of clicks' but the correction never uses that figure. No change needed. An added source supports the experiment claim from the paper body.

fieldFixes.correction: When Nouwens and colleagues scraped the top 10,000 UK websites in September 2019 for the five most popular consent platforms, only 11.8% of the 680 sites using them met three minimal requirements of EU law (explicit consent, rejecting as easy as accepting, no pre-ticked boxes), and half had no 'reject all' button. In their field experiment with 40 participants, removing the 'reject all' button from the first page raised consent by 22-23 percentage points. Interface design, not only preference, shapes how many people click 'yes'.

issues: The figures are right. The crawl is the January 2016 measurement of the Alexa top 1 million: canvas fingerprinting on 14,371 sites (1.6% of the 917,261 sites successfully measured), 98.2% from third-party scripts.

The correction leaves out the paper's own caveat, which weakens how it uses the number as evidence of tracking. On the same page the authors write that 'the most prominent trackers have by-and-large stopped using it' and that 'the use has shifted from behavioral tracking to fraud detection'. Presenting the 14,371 sites as tracking without this is misleading. The fix adds the caveat.

The correction never shows that fingerprinting survives cookie clearing, which is the myth's actual point. The paper says so directly for a device readout (the Battery Status API): 'the readout may remain constant when a user clears cookies'. That quote is added.

'draws hidden graphics' is not what the paper says. It describes devices drawing the same image differently ('Differences in font rendering, smoothing, anti-aliasing ... cause devices to draw the image differently'). The wording is adjusted.

fieldFixes.correction: Tracking also works without stored identifiers. Englehardt and Narayanan's January 2016 crawl of the top million sites found canvas fingerprinting, which identifies a device from the tiny differences in how it draws the same image, on 14,371 sites, 98.2% of it from third-party scripts. The authors noted that its use had shifted from behavioural tracking toward fraud detection, but such fingerprints need no cookie. They warned that another device readout they found in fingerprinting scripts 'may remain constant when a user clears cookies, switches to private browsing mode, or opens a new browser'.

sourceFixes.note: Fresh fetch 2026-09-23, --check FOUND. The paper says: 'In this paper we report results from a January 2016 measurement of the top 1 million sites' (--check FOUND). Table 7 totals '15089 (14371 unique)'. The header reads 'This is an extended version of our paper that appeared at ACM CCS 2016.' The same page also says: 'Third, the use has shifted from behavioral tracking to fraud detection, in line with the ad industry’s self-regulatory norm regarding acceptable uses of ﬁngerprinting.' (--check FOUND with the PDF's ligature)

issues: All four quotes are verbatim on fresh fetches, and the numbers are right: EUR 7.1bn from 25 May 2018 to 10 Jan 2026 (DLA Piper, 21 January 2026); Ireland EUR 4.04bn; Meta EUR 1.2bn in 2023 (CMS dates the decision 12.05.2023); CMS EUR 6.11bn to a 1 March 2026 cut-off.

'concentrated on a few big-tech firms' had no source in the record. The DLA Piper quotes support only the Ireland concentration. The CMS page (already cited) supports it. Its 'Overall top 10 Fines' table lists only Meta Platforms Ireland/Inc. (5 fines), TikTok (2), LinkedIn, Uber and WhatsApp Ireland, and says the Irish DPC accounts for 9 of the top 10. That quote is added.

'slow enforcement' had no source. Added: ICCL's 2021 GDPR report (an advocacy group, Irish Council for Civil Liberties), which says 98% of major cases referred to Ireland were unresolved. It is dated September 2021, so it is framed as a 2021 finding.
DLA Piper's EUR 7.1bn covers 'all the jurisdictions surveyed' (EU/EEA plus UK), which the phrase 'by DLA Piper's count' already covers.

fieldFixes.correction: Fines are real and large: about EUR 7.1 billion from 25 May 2018 to 10 January 2026 by DLA Piper's count, including a single EUR 1.2 billion fine on Meta in 2023. But they are concentrated on a few big-tech firms and a few regulators. Ireland alone accounts for about EUR 4.04 billion, and every one of the ten largest fines in CMS's tracker, nine of them Irish, fell on Meta (including WhatsApp), TikTok, LinkedIn or Uber. Totals also differ by method: CMS counts about EUR 6.11 billion of publicly known fines to 1 March 2026. The fair criticism is uneven, slow enforcement, not absence of enforcement: in 2021 the Irish Council for Civil Liberties found 98% of major GDPR cases referred to Ireland still unresolved.
